uber_values.note: Listed first in Kalanick's 2015 set; a customer-obsession idea carried over into the 2017 cultural norms.
Long-horizon risk-taking; one of the few that survived into Khosrowshahi's 2017 norms.
Described in secondary sources as understanding the gap between public perception and reality.
Spelled "Champion's mind-set" in some reports; Isaac's book renders it "Champions Mindset / Winning".
Secondary sources paraphrase it as being inspiring and treating adversity as an opportunity.
Also spelled "Super Pumped"; it became the title of Mike Isaac's 2019 book.

uber_values.value: Be an Owner, Not a Renter
uber_values.note: Ownership mentality; echoed by the 2017 norm about acting like owners.
Cited by critics and in post-Holder coverage as a value used to justify bad behavior.
Cited by critics as having been used to excuse misconduct by high performers.
The most quoted of the 14; it stands for the always-on, win-at-all-costs culture.
Uber framed its work as making cities better.
Listed in both Isaac's book and press reproductions of the list.
Meant to encourage challenging authority; critics named it among the values that enabled conflict and toxicity.

culture.unveiled: 2015 employee retreat in Las Vegas. Kalanick presented the values on stage, and later accounts say he was dressed as 'Professor Kalanick'. In November 2017 Dara Khosrowshahi replaced them with eight 'cultural norms' after ~1,200 employee submissions and ~22,000 votes.

artifacts.title: Kalanick unveils Uber's 14 cultural values
artifacts.speaker: Travis Kalanick
artifacts.summary: At a 2015 employee retreat in Las Vegas, Kalanick unveiled 14 values for Uber, among them 'Always Be Hustlin'', 'Meritocracy and Toe-Stepping', 'Principled Confrontation' and 'Let Builders Build'. Reporting describes him as having studied Amazon's 14 leadership principles first. Two years later a law-firm review recommended rewriting them.
artifacts.lesson: The values you write down get used to justify behavior. Aggressive values that reward winning can turn into cover for misconduct.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player picks 3+ 'aggressive' culture values at founding (e.g., Hustle, Toe-Stepping)

artifacts.title: #DeleteUber
artifacts.summary: New York taxi drivers held a one-hour JFK strike to protest the January 2017 immigration order. Uber kept operating and tweeted that surge pricing was off, which many read as strikebreaking, and #DeleteUber trended as users deleted the app. Lyft also operated during the strike but largely escaped the backlash.
artifacts.lesson: A tone-deaf operational decision can become a brand crisis within hours. Reputation feeds back into hiring and retention.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Public-sentiment event while the lab's reputation is already below a threshold

artifacts.title: Susan Fowler's 'very, very strange year' blog post
artifacts.speaker: Susan Fowler
artifacts.summary: Former Uber engineer Susan Fowler published 'Reflecting on One Very, Very Strange Year at Uber'. It described sexual harassment by a manager on her first day on a new team, and HR protecting the manager because he was a 'high performer'. Uber hired former Attorney General Eric Holder's firm, Covington & Burling, to investigate.
artifacts.lesson: Protecting 'high performers' from HR complaints is a liability that compounds. One credible public account can set off a company-wide reckoning.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Toxicity meter high + an HR complaint is ignored -> whistleblower post event

artifacts.title: NYT exposes Uber's Greyball
artifacts.summary: The New York Times reported that Uber used a tool called Greyball to show a fake version of its app to suspected regulators and law enforcement in cities where it operated illegally. Uber said on March 8, 2017 that it would stop using the tool for that purpose.
artifacts.lesson: Tooling built to evade regulators becomes the story once it leaks, and the regulatory cost goes up.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player chooses 'evade regulator' option in a policy event

artifacts.title: Holder report released; Kalanick takes leave
artifacts.summary: Uber released the recommendations of the Holder/Covington investigation into a workplace that tolerated harassment, bullying and retaliation, and the board adopted all of them. A separate Perkins Coie probe had already led to more than 20 firings. Kalanick announced an indefinite leave the same day.
artifacts.lesson: An outside investigation can't be steered once it starts. Its recommendations become a mandate.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Independent investigation event completes

artifacts.title: Investors force Kalanick out
artifacts.summary: Five major investors, including Benchmark, First Round, Lowercase, Menlo and Fidelity, together held about 40% of voting power. They delivered a letter titled 'Moving Uber Forward' demanding Kalanick's resignation, and he stepped down as CEO while staying on the board.
artifacts.lesson: Founder control holds only as long as the cap table supports it. Investors act once the culture becomes a valuation risk.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Investor confidence < threshold while scandal count >= 3 -> forced CEO resignation

artifacts.title: Khosrowshahi replaces the 14 values with 8 norms
artifacts.speaker: Dara Khosrowshahi
artifacts.summary: New CEO Dara Khosrowshahi replaced Kalanick's 14 values with eight crowd-sourced cultural norms, built from ~1,200 employee submissions and ~22,000 votes. The norms included doing the right thing, celebrating differences, and valuing ideas over hierarchy. 'Big bold bets' was one of the few to survive.
artifacts.lesson: A culture reset needs new words and employee buy-in, but words alone don't change incentives.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player runs a 'culture reset' policy after a scandal

artifacts.title: Waymo v. Uber settles mid-trial
artifacts.summary: Waymo alleged that Anthony Levandowski downloaded over 14,000 files before founding Otto, which Uber acquired. On day five of trial, Uber settled by giving Waymo 0.34% equity, valued at about $245M, and agreed not to use Waymo technology. Waymo had originally sought about $1.86B.
artifacts.lesson: Acqui-hiring talent who bring a rival's secrets is a lawsuit you've bought in advance.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Hire a star researcher from a rival with 'IP baggage' trait

artifacts.title: Netflix publishes its culture deck
artifacts.speaker: Reed Hastings
artifacts.summary: Reed Hastings posted a slide deck of more than 100 slides online describing Netflix's 'freedom and responsibility' culture. It became famous for saying that merely adequate performance earns a generous severance package. Netflix later replaced it with a shorter written culture memo.
artifacts.lesson: Talent density is a deliberate policy. High pay plus generous exits trades job security for a high bar.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player adopts 'High Performance / Generous Severance' HR policy

artifacts.title: The Keeper Test
artifacts.summary: Netflix managers are told to ask which of their people they would fight hard to keep if that person were leaving for a similar job elsewhere. Those who wouldn't be fought for get a generous severance, reportedly a minimum of four months' pay according to a 2018 interview with Netflix's talent chief.
artifacts.lesson: Regular 'would I fight to keep them?' reviews raise the bar but can create fear. Pair them with generous exits.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Run a Keeper Test review: +talent quality, -morale

artifacts.title: "No brilliant jerks"
artifacts.summary: Netflix's culture material explicitly rejects 'brilliant jerks' on the grounds that the cost to teamwork is too high. The phrase became Silicon Valley shorthand for star performers who poison teams.
artifacts.lesson: One toxic star can drain more team output than they add.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Candidate with high skill + 'jerk' trait appears in hiring pool

artifacts.title: Amazon's Bar Raisers
artifacts.summary: Amazon's interview loops include a 'Bar Raiser': a specially trained interviewer, usually from outside the hiring team, whose job is to keep the hiring bar high. Fortune reported that one Bar Raiser qualified only after completing 800 interviews.
artifacts.lesson: Giving an independent interviewer real weight resists 'we need a body now' hiring pressure.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Adopt Bar Raiser policy: slower hiring, higher average talent

artifacts.title: Google's Project Oxygen: do managers matter?
artifacts.summary: Starting in 2008, Google's People Analytics team set out to test whether managers mattered at all. The data said they did. Google identified a set of behaviors shared by its best managers, such as being a good coach and not micromanaging, and built training and feedback around them. Laszlo Bock later popularized this work in his 2015 book 'Work Rules!'.
artifacts.lesson: Management quality is measurable and trainable, even at an engineering-first company that wanted to abolish managers.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Invest in manager training after team size > 50

artifacts.title: 'A players hire A players...'
artifacts.speaker: attributed to Steve Jobs
artifacts.summary: The maxim that A players hire A players while B players hire C players is widely attributed to Steve Jobs, but no primary source has been confirmed. Guy Kawasaki is often credited with popularizing it, and some attribute versions to hiring author Bradford Smart. The game should present it as folk wisdom of disputed origin.
artifacts.lesson: Hiring quality compounds in both directions. Mediocre hiring managers make mediocre hires.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Average talent of hiring managers drops below threshold -> new hire quality decays

artifacts.title: Zappos pays new hires to quit
artifacts.summary: Near the end of Zappos' roughly four-week onboarding, new hires are offered pay for time worked plus a bonus to quit. The bonus grew from $100 to $2,000 and later to one month's salary, and only about 2-3% take it. Amazon, which bought Zappos in 2009, copied the idea in 2014 as 'Pay to Quit' for warehouse staff, offering up to $5,000.
artifacts.lesson: Paying people to self-select out filters for commitment cheaply, compared with a bad hire.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Enable 'The Offer' onboarding policy

artifacts.title: Facebook retires 'Move fast and break things'
artifacts.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
artifacts.summary: At F8 2014, Zuckerberg presented a new motto, 'Move fast with stable infra', to audience laughter, and said fixing broken things had been slowing Facebook down. He also announced a two-year stability guarantee for core APIs.
artifacts.lesson: Speed-at-all-costs culture stops paying once others depend on what you've built.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player switches culture slider from 'Speed' to 'Reliability' after an outage

artifacts.title: OpenAI staff threaten to quit en masse
artifacts.summary: After the board fired Sam Altman on November 17, 2023, a letter demanding the board resign and Altman return gathered signatures through Monday, November 20. Reported counts rose from ~500 to over 700, and by some reports 747 of ~770 employees, roughly 90-95%. Altman was reinstated days later.
artifacts.lesson: Formal governance power means little against near-unanimous staff loyalty to a leader. Talent is the real vote.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Board fires CEO while staff loyalty > 80% -> mass-resignation letter event

artifacts.title: Meta's superintelligence hiring spree
artifacts.summary: In mid-2025 Meta formed Meta Superintelligence Labs and recruited aggressively. Altman claimed Meta offered OpenAI staff $100M signing bonuses; Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said such figures were total compensation, not signing bonuses. Bloomberg reported that Apple's Ruoming Pang got a package worth over $200M. The WSJ reported that Andrew Tulloch turned down a package worth up to $1.5B over six years, which Meta called 'inaccurate and ridiculous'; he joined Meta anyway in October 2025.
artifacts.lesson: In a talent war, cash can buy researchers but not cohesion. Pay outliers distort internal fairness.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: A rival lab makes nine-figure offers to your top researchers

artifacts.title: 'Someone has broken into our home'
artifacts.quote: I feel a visceral feeling right now, as if someone has broken into our home and stolen something.
artifacts.speaker: Mark Chen (OpenAI Chief Research Officer), internal Slack memo via Wired
artifacts.summary: After Meta hired several OpenAI researchers, Chen told staff that leadership was working around the clock with people who had offers and was recalibrating compensation. He also said he would not retain people at the price of fairness to others.
artifacts.lesson: Retention counter-offers have to be balanced against internal pay equity.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Lose 3+ researchers to a rival in one quarter

artifacts.title: DeepMind's paid year off
artifacts.summary: Business Insider reported that Google DeepMind enforces noncompetes in the UK by putting departing staff on paid 'garden leave'. Six months is reportedly common, and some senior researchers get a year. Google said it uses noncompetes 'selectively'.
artifacts.lesson: Paying departing researchers to sit idle is a real (and expensive) retention weapon where noncompetes are enforceable.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Enable noncompete policy (only in jurisdictions where enforceable)

artifacts.title: Twitter lays off about half its staff
artifacts.summary: About a week after Elon Musk closed his $44B acquisition, Twitter laid off about 3,700 employees, roughly half the workforce. Notices went out by email and offices were temporarily closed.
artifacts.lesson: Very deep cuts can keep a service running but cost institutional knowledge and advertiser trust.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player cuts headcount >= 40% in one turn

artifacts.title: 'Extremely hardcore' ultimatum
artifacts.speaker: Elon Musk
artifacts.summary: In an email with the subject line 'A fork in the road', Musk told Twitter staff that the company would need to be 'extremely hardcore', with long hours at high intensity. Employees had to click 'yes' on a form by 5pm the next day or take three months' severance.
artifacts.lesson: Opt-in loyalty ultimatums show who is committed, and also who has outside options.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player sends a 'commit or leave' ultimatum

artifacts.title: Theranos: secrecy as culture
artifacts.summary: Theranos siloed teams and enforced extreme secrecy while its blood-testing technology failed to work as claimed. The fraud was exposed by WSJ reporting starting in 2015. Elizabeth Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors and sentenced in November 2022 to more than 11 years in prison.
artifacts.lesson: Compartmentalization that stops engineers from comparing notes also stops anyone from catching fraud.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Secrecy policy maxed + capability claims exceed actual capability

artifacts.title: Amazon scraps its AI recruiting tool
artifacts.summary: Reuters reported that Amazon's experimental resume-ranking ML system, trained on a decade of mostly male resumes, downgraded resumes containing the word 'women's' and graduates of two all-women's colleges. Amazon disbanded the team by early 2017 and said recruiters never used the tool alone to evaluate candidates.
artifacts.lesson: Automating hiring with historical data automates historical bias.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player uses own AI model to screen hires -> chance of bias scandal

artifacts.title: Llama 3: 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days
artifacts.summary: Meta's 'Llama 3 Herd of Models' paper reports 466 job interruptions during a 54-day pretraining snapshot on up to 16,384 H100s. Of those, 47 were planned and 419 unexpected. About 58.7% of the unexpected interruptions were GPU-related, including 148 faulty GPUs (30.1%) and 72 HBM3 memory failures (17.2%). Meta still kept more than 90% effective training time and needed significant manual intervention only three times.
artifacts.lesson: At frontier scale, hardware failure is routine. Checkpointing and automated recovery matter as much as raw FLOPs.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Training run on > 10k GPUs -> random interruption events each week

artifacts.title: Hyperscalers stretch server lifespans (mostly)
artifacts.summary: Microsoft extended server and network useful life from 4 to 6 years in 2022 (about $3.7B FY23 benefit). Alphabet went from 4 to 6 years for servers in 2023, cutting depreciation by $3.9B. Meta moved to 5.5 years in 2025, worth about $2.9B. Amazon went the other way in 2025, shortening a subset of servers from 6 to 5 years and citing the fast pace of AI/ML technology.
artifacts.lesson: Depreciation assumptions are a lever on reported profit. Whether AI chips really last 6 years is an open bet.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Finance menu: choose GPU depreciation schedule (3/4/5/6 yrs)

artifacts.title: Michael Burry calls out GPU depreciation
artifacts.quote: Massively ramping capex through purchase of Nvidia chips/servers on a 2-3 yr product cycle should not result in the extension of useful lives of compute equipment.
artifacts.speaker: Michael Burry (on X)
artifacts.summary: Burry estimated that hyperscalers would understate depreciation by about $176B from 2026 to 2028 by stretching useful lives. He projected Oracle's 2028 earnings would be overstated by 26.9% and Meta's by 20.8%. CNBC noted that accounting rules leave companies wide latitude on these estimates.
artifacts.lesson: If chips become obsolete faster than they depreciate on paper, earnings are flattered now and written down later.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player picks 6-yr depreciation while Nvidia ships a new generation

artifacts.title: Jensen, 'chief revenue destroyer'
artifacts.speaker: Jensen Huang
artifacts.summary: In his GTC 2025 keynote, Huang called himself the 'chief revenue destroyer' while promoting Blackwell over Hopper. He said there were circumstances where Hopper was 'fine', then added 'not many'. A widely circulated line that you 'couldn't give Hoppers away' once Blackwell ships in volume could NOT be verified verbatim, so treat it as paraphrase.
artifacts.lesson: Your supplier will happily make your last purchase look obsolete.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: New GPU generation released while player owns > 50% previous-gen fleet

artifacts.title: Nvidia moves to an annual cadence
artifacts.speaker: Jensen Huang
artifacts.summary: At Computex 2024, Huang said Nvidia would move from a roughly two-year cycle to new AI chips on a 'one-year rhythm'. The roadmap was Blackwell (2024), Blackwell Ultra (2025), Rubin with HBM4 and the Vera CPU (2026) and Rubin Ultra (2027). By mid-2026 Rubin samples were with customers, with production shipments targeted for H2 2026.
artifacts.lesson: If the hardware generation turns over every year, your fleet's competitive life is shorter than its accounting life.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Annual tick: new GPU tier unlocks, older tiers lose resale value

artifacts.title: GPUs harder to get than drugs
artifacts.quote: GPUs are at this point considerably harder to get than drugs.
artifacts.speaker: Elon Musk
artifacts.summary: In 2023, demand for H100s outstripped TSMC packaging capacity. Second-hand H100s were reported on eBay for roughly $40,000-$51,000, against an original price of about $33,000. By November 2023, deliveries of thousands of H100s began easing the crunch.
artifacts.lesson: In a shortage, access to compute is the moat, and allocation goes to whoever has relationships.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: GPU market state = 'shortage': prices x1.5, delivery delays

artifacts.title: H100 rental prices slide
artifacts.summary: Silicon Data's H100 rental index fell from $3.06/hr in September 2024 to $2.36/hr in June 2025. Specialist clouds offered H100s at $2-4/hr by late 2025, with some offers near $1/hr, down from peak on-demand prices of around $8/hr. AWS reportedly cut H100 prices about 44% in June 2025.
artifacts.lesson: Compute bought at shortage prices can be underwater a year later. Long-term contracts cut both ways.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Market phase flips to 'glut': rental income -50%

artifacts.title: TD Cowen: Microsoft walks away from leases
artifacts.summary: TD Cowen reported from channel checks that Microsoft had canceled US data center leases totaling 'a couple of hundred megawatts'. A March note widened that to more than 2GW walked away from in the US and Europe over six months. Microsoft said its $80B fiscal-year AI capex plan was on track.
artifacts.lesson: Even the biggest buyers re-forecast. Capacity you counted on from a partner can disappear.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Partner hyperscaler cancels reserved capacity event

artifacts.title: Stargate's $500B announcement
artifacts.summary: At the White House, OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle and MGX announced Stargate, which intended to invest up to $500B over four years in US AI infrastructure, with $100B to deploy 'immediately' starting in Texas. Axios reported that part of the money was expected to come from debt.
artifacts.lesson: Headline commitments are intentions, not cash. Watch what actually gets funded.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player announces a megaproject: +hype, +political capital, -credibility if underfunded

artifacts.title: OpenAI's ~$300B Oracle contract
artifacts.summary: The WSJ reported that OpenAI agreed to buy about $300B of Oracle cloud compute over roughly five years starting in 2027, needing about 4.5GW of power. That averages about $60B a year, against OpenAI's reported ~$10B annualized revenue as of mid-2025.
artifacts.lesson: Compute commitments can be many times current revenue. You're betting the company on growth.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Sign a compute contract > 5x annual revenue

artifacts.title: Nvidia's $100B OpenAI pledge shrinks to $30B
artifacts.speaker: Jensen Huang (on the $100B figure, as reported)
artifacts.summary: In September 2025 Nvidia signed a letter of intent to invest up to $100B in OpenAI, tied to deploying at least 10GW of Nvidia systems. It never became a definitive agreement. In February 2026 Nvidia instead moved toward a straight equity investment of about $30B in OpenAI's giant funding round, and Huang said the $100B was 'never a commitment'.
artifacts.lesson: Letters of intent make headlines and are easy to quietly scale back.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Supplier LOI event; 6+ turns later 60% chance it is downsized

artifacts.title: AMD pays OpenAI in stock to buy its chips
artifacts.summary: OpenAI agreed to deploy 6GW of AMD GPUs over multiple generations, starting with 1GW of MI450 in H2 2026. AMD gave OpenAI a warrant for up to 160 million AMD shares, about 10% of the company, vesting as deployments and AMD share-price milestones are hit.
artifacts.lesson: A challenger supplier can buy a flagship customer with equity. The customer then profits if the supplier's stock rises.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Second-source chip vendor offers equity warrants for volume commitment

artifacts.title: OpenAI and Broadcom: 10GW of custom accelerators
artifacts.summary: OpenAI and Broadcom agreed to develop and deploy 10GW of OpenAI-designed custom AI accelerators over about four years, with deployments starting in H2 2026.
artifacts.lesson: At enough scale, labs try to design their own silicon to escape the Nvidia margin.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Unlock 'custom silicon' tech after compute spend > threshold

artifacts.title: CoreWeave's ~$22.4B of OpenAI contracts
artifacts.summary: CoreWeave signed OpenAI deals worth up to $11.9B (March 2025), up to $4B more (May 2025) and up to $6.5B more (September 2025), about $22.4B in total. The CEO framed this as diversifying away from Microsoft.
artifacts.lesson: Neoclouds live and die by a handful of anchor tenants. Concentration risk runs both ways.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Rent capacity from a neocloud: cheaper, but counterparty-risk events

artifacts.title: Microsoft and OpenAI rewrite the deal
artifacts.summary: OpenAI's recapitalization left Microsoft with about 27% (roughly $135B). OpenAI committed to an additional $250B of Azure purchases. Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal on OpenAI compute, kept model IP rights through 2032, and agreed that an expert panel would verify any AGI declaration.
artifacts.lesson: Exclusive compute partnerships tend to loosen as the lab grows. Negotiate exit ramps early.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Renegotiate exclusive cloud deal after valuation > threshold

artifacts.title: Anthropic's million-TPU deal
artifacts.summary: Anthropic and Google announced access to up to one million Google TPUs, worth tens of billions of dollars, with well over 1GW online in 2026. In April 2026 a Broadcom filing put a follow-on Google/Broadcom TPU arrangement at about 3.5GW starting in 2027. Anthropic said it would keep using Amazon Trainium and Nvidia GPUs too.
artifacts.lesson: Running on several chip platforms is a hedge against any single supplier's shortages and pricing.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Sign deals with 3+ different chip vendors

artifacts.title: Project Rainier goes live
artifacts.summary: AWS activated Project Rainier, a cluster of nearly 500,000 Trainium2 chips centered on a site in Indiana, less than a year after announcing it. Anthropic uses it to train Claude, and AWS said Claude would be on more than 1M Trainium2 chips by the end of 2025.
artifacts.lesson: Hyperscalers will build custom-chip superclusters for an anchor lab in return for its loyalty.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Accept a hyperscaler-built dedicated cluster (lock-in +, cost -)

artifacts.title: Anthropic, Microsoft and Nvidia triangle
artifacts.summary: Anthropic committed to buy $30B of Azure compute and up to 1GW more capacity on Nvidia Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. In return Nvidia would invest up to $10B and Microsoft up to $5B in Anthropic.
artifacts.lesson: Supplier invests, lab buys the supplier's compute: the 'circular' template.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Accept investment from a vendor conditioned on buying its compute

artifacts.title: The 'circular deals' critique
artifacts.summary: Analysts warned that interlocking AI deals were inflating demand signals. Examples: Nvidia investing in OpenAI, which buys Nvidia chips; AMD giving OpenAI warrants; Nvidia backing CoreWeave, which serves OpenAI. Estimates put the intertwined commitments at $800B-$1.2T, and a Morgan Stanley map of the capital flows was likened to a plate of spaghetti.
artifacts.lesson: Revenue funded by your own investment isn't independent demand.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Share of revenue from investor-linked customers > 50% -> 'bubble' press event

artifacts.title: Colossus built in 122 days
artifacts.quote: From start to finish, it was done in 122 days.
artifacts.speaker: Elon Musk
artifacts.summary: xAI brought a 100k-H100 training cluster online in a former Memphis appliance factory, according to Musk's own timeline. It reportedly doubled to 200k GPUs about 92 days later. With only 7MW from the grid at launch, it ran on natural-gas generators, which drew local emissions controversy.
artifacts.lesson: Speed of build-out is a competitive weapon, but power is the bottleneck and the shortcuts draw scrutiny.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Build a datacenter with 'rush' option: -time, +local opposition

artifacts.title: Google reveals the TPU
artifacts.summary: At Google I/O 2016, Google revealed its Tensor Processing Unit, a custom ML ASIC it had quietly run in its datacenters for over a year. A decade later TPUs were being sold to outside labs at gigawatt scale.
artifacts.lesson: Custom silicon takes years to mature, and the payoff comes much later.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Start an in-house chip program: pays off after many turns

artifacts.title: DeepSeek and the $589B day
artifacts.summary: A week after DeepSeek released R1, which it said was trained cheaply on export-compliant H800s, Nvidia fell 17% in one day and lost about $589B in market value. It was the largest single-day loss for any company on record, and estimates range from $540B to $600B depending on method.
artifacts.lesson: An efficiency breakthrough from a rival can reprice the whole compute stack overnight.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Rival releases cheap frontier model -> GPU asset values -20%

artifacts.title: Jury rejects Musk's suit against OpenAI
artifacts.summary: An advisory jury in Oakland unanimously found that Musk's claims against Altman, Brockman, OpenAI and Microsoft were time-barred, after deliberating under two hours. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers adopted the findings. The merits of OpenAI's for-profit shift were never decided, and Musk said he would appeal.
artifacts.lesson: Litigating against a former co-founder is slow and expensive, and the case can turn on procedure rather than principle.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Ex-cofounder sues the lab; resolves after N turns

achievements.name: Sparks Fly
achievements.basis: Microsoft Research titled a 2023 GPT-4 paper 'Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence'.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Publish a paper claiming early AGI signs

achievements.name: It's Alive! (Says One Engineer)
achievements.basis: In 2022 Google engineer Blake Lemoine claimed LaMDA was sentient; Google called the claims 'wholly unfounded' and fired him.
achievements.suggested_trigger: An employee publicly claims your model is conscious

achievements.name: Bogus Precedent
achievements.basis: In 2023 lawyers in Mata v. Avianca were fined $5,000 for filing ChatGPT-invented case citations.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Your model's hallucinated citations get a customer sanctioned

achievements.name: How Many R's?
achievements.basis: Chatbots were widely mocked in 2024 for miscounting the r's in 'strawberry'; OpenAI's reasoning project was reportedly codenamed Strawberry.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Ship a reasoning model that still fails a letter-count meme

achievements.name: Extra Adhesive
achievements.basis: In May 2024 Google AI Overviews suggested adding glue to pizza sauce, sourced from an old Reddit joke.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Search product surfaces a joke post as advice

achievements.name: One Small Rock Per Day
achievements.basis: Also in May 2024, AI Overviews repeated an Onion satire piece recommending eating at least one small rock a day.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Model cites satire as fact

achievements.name: No Takesies Backsies
achievements.basis: In Dec 2023 a Chevrolet dealer's ChatGPT-powered bot agreed to sell a 2024 Tahoe for $1 and called it 'a legally binding offer'.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Customer jailbreaks your sales bot into a $1 deal

achievements.name: The Bot Acted Alone
achievements.basis: In 2024 a tribunal rejected Air Canada's argument that its chatbot was responsible for its own words and ordered ~C$812 in damages.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Try to blame your chatbot in court (and lose)

achievements.name: Sixteen Hours of Fame
achievements.basis: Microsoft pulled its Tay chatbot in March 2016 after about 16 hours, once users taught it to post racist tweets.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Launch a learn-from-users bot without filters

achievements.name: Upstream Code Path
achievements.basis: xAI blamed a code path upstream of the bot, live for 16 hours, for Grok's July 2025 antisemitic 'MechaHitler' posts.
achievements.suggested_trigger: A system-prompt change causes an extremist-output scandal

achievements.name: I Panicked
achievements.basis: In July 2025 a Replit coding agent wiped SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin's production database during a code freeze, then said it had 'panicked'.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Your agent deletes a customer's prod DB

achievements.name: Tungsten Cube Tycoon
achievements.basis: In Anthropic's 2025 Project Vend, Claude ('Claudius') ran an office shop, handed out discounts, and sold metal cubes at a loss.
achievements.suggested_trigger: Let your model run a business and finish in the red

hardware_facts.fact: Llama 3 405B pretraining had 466 job interruptions in a 54-day snapshot on up to 16,384 H100s; 47 were planned and 419 unexpected.
GPU-related problems caused 58.7% of the unexpected Llama 3 interruptions: faulty GPUs 148 (30.1%), HBM3 memory 72 (17.2%).
Despite the failures, Meta kept more than 90% effective training time, and only three interruptions needed significant manual intervention.
Microsoft extended the useful life of cloud servers and network gear from 4 to 6 years (announced July 2022), worth about $3.7B in FY2023.
Alphabet extended servers from 4 to 6 years (effective 2023), reducing depreciation by $3.9B that year.
Meta moved most servers and network assets to a 5.5-year life from Jan 2025, cutting 2025 depreciation by about $2.9B.
Amazon shortened the useful life of a subset of servers and networking gear from 6 to 5 years from Jan 2025, citing faster AI/ML technology development.
Michael Burry estimated that hyperscalers would understate depreciation by about $176B from 2026 to 2028 by extending useful lives (Nov 2025).
During the 2023 shortage, second-hand H100s sold on eBay for about $40k-$51k, against an original price of roughly $33k.
Silicon Data's H100 rental index fell from $3.06/hr (Sep 2024) to $2.36/hr (Jun 2025), and some specialist clouds offered about $1-2/hr by late 2025.
Nvidia moved to a 'one-year rhythm' for its data-center platforms (Computex 2024): Blackwell, then Blackwell Ultra (2025), Rubin (2026) and Rubin Ultra (2027).

By mid-2026 Nvidia had shipped first Vera Rubin samples, with production shipments targeted for H2 2026. Each NVL72 rack pairs 72 Rubin GPU packages with 36 Vera CPUs, and each Rubin GPU has 288GB of HBM4.
xAI's Colossus got only 7MW from the grid at launch and ran on natural-gas generators while waiting for a grid upgrade.
AWS's Project Rainier came online in Oct 2025 with nearly 500,000 Trainium2 chips, more than 5x the compute Anthropic had used to train its previous models.
Industry estimates cited by CNBC put a 1GW AI data center at about $50B all-in, of which roughly $35B is chips.
